title: Stanley's First-Ever Diwali Collection Pairs Festival Motifs With a 50-Year-Old Bangalore Studio
excerpt: The Deepa Rose and Deepa Brown Sugar line, designed with Padmini Govind of Tharangini Studio, spans $35-$68 and lands a month before Diwali begins on November 6.
body:
• Stanley 1913 has launched its first-ever Diwali Collection, a limited-edition drinkware line inspired by the Festival of Lights, released October 6 exclusively on the Stanley website.
  • The collection comes in two colourways — Deepa Rose and Deepa Brown Sugar — designed with Padmini Govind of Tharangini Studio, a women-led block-printing studio in Bangalore celebrating its 50th anniversary this year.
  • Patterns are drawn from Tharangini's vintage archives, including a mango-leaf paisley significant in Diwali rituals and henna motifs.
  • The five-piece line spans $35 to $68, from the 16-ounce Café-to-Go Mug to the 1-quart New Legend Vacuum Bottle — landing a month before Diwali, which begins November 6 this year.

The Stanley cup has officially gone desi. Stanley 1913 has unveiled its first-ever Diwali Collection — a limited-edition line of tumblers, bottles and mugs designed around the Festival of Lights, and built with an Indian artisan studio at its creative core.

The collection, which launched October 6 exclusively on Stanley's website, comes in two colourways: Deepa Rose and Deepa Brown Sugar. The name is the giveaway — "deepa" is the Sanskrit word for light, the essence of the five-day festival that honours new beginnings and the triumph of light over darkness.

A Bangalore studio at the centre

"The name is the giveaway — "deepa" is the Sanskrit word for light, the essence of the five-day festival that honours new beginnings and the triumph of light over darkness."

The designs were created with Padmini Govind of Tharangini Studio, a women-led block-printing studio in Bangalore that has been producing sustainable textiles since the mid-1970s and is celebrating its 50th anniversary this year. According to Stanley, the patterns come from Tharangini's "rare and vintage archives," including a paisley resembling a mango leaf — a motif with specific significance in Diwali rituals — alongside henna-inspired designs.

This is not Stanley's first artisan collaboration. The brand's Día de Muertos collection, created with the nonprofit Nest that supports artisan businesses in over 120 countries, sold out in minutes last year. The playbook is now familiar: pair a beloved seasonal festival with genuine craft heritage, release in limited quantities, and let collectors do the rest.

The line-up

The Diwali collection spans five formats: the 30-ounce Quencher ProTour ($50), the 20-ounce Flowstate Spring Bottle ($40), the 1-quart New Legend Vacuum Bottle ($68), the 16-ounce Café-to-Go Mug ($35), and a Stacking Cup Set ($50). The timing is deliberate — Diwali begins Friday, November 6 this year, putting the launch a full month ahead of the festival and squarely in the gifting window.

Why it matters

For a brand whose cultural footprint was built on American suburban mom culture and TikTok virality, a Diwali collection designed with a 50-year-old Bangalore textile studio is a meaningful acknowledgement of where its customers actually are. The Indian diaspora is one of the most enthusiastic consumer cohorts for festival-season limited editions, and Diwali gifting — sweets, dry fruits, and now apparently heirloom-grade tumblers — is a serious retail season.

There is a real question underneath the marketing: whether this is cultural appreciation or appropriation-by-collaboration. On the evidence, Stanley has done this one right — crediting the studio by name, drawing from its actual archives, and putting a working artisan (not a mood board) at the centre of the story. The Tharangini partnership gives the collection a provenance that most festival-themed merchandise lacks.

What to watch

Limited-edition Stanley drops have a habit of selling out fast — the Día de Muertos line vanished in minutes. If the Diwali collection follows the pattern, expect resale markups within days of launch. The more interesting signal will be whether Stanley makes this an annual franchise: a brand that does Diwali once is dabbling; a brand that returns to Tharangini next year is committed.
